The memory, appraisal, threat, and coping items all center on bodily pain, fragmented accident memory, hypervigilance, self-blame, and safety behaviors, but do not provide a plausible bridge from an accident trauma to these interpersonal/child-related triggers.

vignette: Arthur Vance was six months from the end of his final term as a state senator when his sedan hydroplaned off the interstate, the guardrail giving way with a sickening crunch that threw him against the steering wheel. In that collision, the trauma did not unfold as a continuous narrative for him; instead, it fractured into a handful of frozen pictures: the sudden glass bloom, the angle of the dashboard, the terrifying stillness that followed. Because Arthur had come to believe that the crash happened to him because of the sort of person he is, that unshakeable negative appraisal instantly turned his nervous system into a surveillance state. He had to be on guard all the time, scanning every room for danger, which meant his mind would fracture into those same vivid snapshots the moment any familiar discomfort settled in his chest or when he caught the sharp tang of spilled whiskey at a donor dinner. Each olfactory cue instantly pulled the frozen images forward, which directly drove his decision to refuse to drive or even sit in a passenger seat. The sudden sense of physical discomfort or the sharp tang of spilled whiskey at a donor dinner instantly convinced him he was fundamentally flawed and exposed to others’ scrutiny, while his conviction that he was fundamentally exposed to others’ scrutiny made him flee charity galas, which in turn sharpened his sensitivity to any sudden discomfort. As the memory of the impact sharpened, it convinced him that he was fundamentally flawed and that the man who had navigated crises for decades had been reduced to a series of frozen pictures. Over the following months, the negative appraisals about his moral exposure and inherent danger forced him to wake during the night to check whether he was safe, pacing the hallway while unusual silence made him feel something dangerous was about to happen. This waking alert naturally amplified his concentration difficulties, which only made the frozen pictures feel more visceral, which directly drove his decision to refuse to drive or even sit in a passenger seat. When he tried to explain the collision to his wife, he would lose the thread and cannot finish, his voice trailing off as the memory’s physical pain recall returned, his shoulders and ribs aching exactly as they had during the crash. Avoiding the vehicle did not silence his internal alarms; instead, the absence of exposure allowed the snapshot memories to press harder against his chest. When unusual silence made him feel something dangerous was about to happen, it sharpened his awareness of any sudden discomfort. As the memory of the impact sharpened, it left him unable to concentrate and forced him to wake during the night to check whether he was safe. His repeated dwelling on what he had done wrong became the lens through which he interpreted every social interaction, convincing him that the event happened because of the sort of person he is, while his relentless rumination naturally amplified his waking alert, ensuring he would wake during the night to check his surroundings. His relentless rumination naturally funneled his attention back toward environmental cues, causing the sight of cars hit by accident or the sudden sense of physical discomfort to dominate his daily routine. At sixty-eight, Arthur no longer feared the accident itself; what frightened him most was the certainty that he was losing his mind, that he could never again trust his own judgment behind the wheel. He finally sought help after a town hall Q&A where a constituent’s casual mention of a recent fender-bender sent him out the back exit, leaving his speech unfinished and his campaign manager bewildered. He hoped someone could help him quiet the internal alarm before his marriage, already strained by years of empty passenger seats and sleepless nights, fractured beyond repair.
